party.description: The New Zealand Labour Party (Rōpū Reipa o Aotearoa) is a centre-left social democratic party. Its program emphasises the incremental expansion in the role of government in the economy to address poverty and inequality. It currently has 34 seats in parliament. Formed in 1916 by Trade Unions and Socialist political parties, it is historically responsible for much of the modern welfare system. It has held seats in every Parliament since winning 8 in 1919, forming its first government in 1935. Since then, Labour has formed governments on 6 different occasions. Chris Hipkins is the party leader, and its 2026 slogan is ‘Better Starts Now.”
party.name: Labour Party

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that that last year, 155,000 New Zealanders didn't collect medicine they had been prescribed because they couldn't afford it. Not receiving treatments mean that health problems are exacerbated, and research shows that people who skip medication are more likely to end up in hospital. Making prescriptions free is an upfront cost for the government which removes pressure on the health system.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would remove the $5 fee for prescriptions of funded medication. This would apply to anyone who is entitled to free healthcare in New Zealand, instead of just people under age 14 and over age 65 and those with Community Services Cards. This would cost $74.5m a year, funded by a capital gains tax.  This party estimates that this policy would cost $74.5 m a year.

citations.title: 'Free Prescriptions Under Labour', undated (accessed 11 August 2026)

policies.statement: Remove $5 charge for prescriptions

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that many New Zealanders have to choose between medical care and other essentials like food. Some general practices charge nearly $100 per visit. Under the "Medicard" policy programme, anyone eligible for funded healthcare could go to the GP for free at least three times a year. This would be paid for by a capital gains tax.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would cover three visits a year to a doctor or nurse at the GP clinic where people are enrolled. Already free services like immunisations would not count towards the three-visit total. The "Medicard" card and app would link visits to people's National Health Index number. The three free visits are for each year and do not accumulate and roll over into the next year.  This party estimates that this policy would cost $393.3 million in 2027/28, rising to around $553 million a year once fully in place.

citations.title: 'Free Doctor's Visits with the Medicard', undated (accessed 11 August 2026)

policies.statement: Make up to three GP visits a year free

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that NZ is one of the few countries in the world without some form of capital gains tax. Much of New Zealand's wealth is held in property rather than enabling economic growth. A capital gains tax would increase New Zealand's productivity and make housing more affordable. Money raised from the tax would be invested in healthcare.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would introduce a 28% tax on commercial properties and residential investment properties. Family farms, homes, KiwiSaver, shares, business assets, inheritances, gifts, and personal items would be exempt. The tax would only apply to people who own multiple properties or commercial properties, and only to profits made after 1 June 2027.

citations.title: 'Capital Gains Tax', undated (accessed 13 August 2026)

policies.statement: Create a 28% capital gains tax on commercial and residential properties, excluding family homes

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that a cap on public transport fares will help address the everyday struggles New Zealanders face as a result of a high cost of living.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would introduce a weekly fare cap of $20 on public transport in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch. Everywhere else in New Zealand would see a weekly fare cap of $10. This would begin on 1 July 2027. Once the caps are reached, the rest of that week's trips would be free. There would be no sign-up required; transport users would use their public transport card or payment method as usual for public buses and trains and some ferries.

citations.title: 'Labour's $20 Public Transport Fare Cap', undated (accessed 11 August 2026)
'Labour to deliver unlimited public transport for $20-max a week', 10 June 2026 (accessed 24 August 2026)

policies.statement: Introduce a $20 weekly fare cap on public transport

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that that pregnant people should not have to worry about money to know their baby is healthy, with each scan currently costing an average $90. No mum would have to skip a scan because they can't afford it.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would make every referred maternity scan by a doctor, midwife or specialist free in NZ. All a pregnant person would need is a Medicard. To grow the relevant workforce and ease the pressure on hospitals, 24 paid trainee sonographer positions would also be funded, costing less than $3 million a year. This policy would be funded by the party's targeted capital gains tax.  This party estimates that this policy would cost $28.6 million a year.

citations.title: 'Free Maternity Scans with Medicard', undated (accessed 11 August 2026)

policies.statement: Ensure all referred maternity scans are free

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says record numbers of New Zealanders are moving overseas in search of better opportunities. This fund would invest in infrastructure and back innovative NZ businesses.  It would create secure, well-paid jobs, enticing people to stay and build their lives in NZ, in turn, growing the economy.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would establish the fund with a foundation of existing government assets and an initial capital contribution, sitting alongside but separate from the New Zealand Super Fund. It would be independently governed by the Guardians of the Super Fund, with the Minister of Finance as sole shareholder. Some assets would be protected in law to remain under continual public ownership. Other assets would require Ministerial approval before being sold.

citations.title: 'New Zealand Future Fund', undated (accessed 11 August 2026)

policies.statement: Create a fund to invest in infrastructure and businesses

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that that cervical cancer is one of the most preventable cancers but 85 percent of those diagnosed have never been screened or have missed screenings. Free cervical screening means earlier diagnosis, less pressure on hospitals and more lives saved.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would implement free cervical screening for everyone aged 25-69 from 1 October 2027. People's eligibility would be automatically loaded onto the Medicard, with screening available at their local doctor or community screening event. This would be funded from existing health budgets and would be in addition to the three free doctor's visits a year.  This party estimates that this policy would cost $21.6 million for the first full year.

citations.title: 'Free Cervical Screening', undated (accessed 13 August 2026)

policies.statement: Implement free cervical screening for everyone aged 25-69

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that doctors cannot always afford to buy their own practice. Yet private family doctors form the bulk of general practitioners in the health system. If more GPs can afford to open a practice in their local community, it will lower waiting times to see doctors and ease the pressure on busy hospitals.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would introduce a Family Doctor Loan Scheme providing up to 90% of the cost of buying into a practice. This would cap at $500,000 and would be interest-free for the first two years. A 3 percent annual interest rate would apply after that, with 10 years allowed to repay. Up to 50 loans would be available per year for owner-operated general practices. Funding would be supplied through the existing Small Business Cashflow Loan Scheme. This party estimates that this policy would cost $25 million a year if fully subscribed.

citations.title: 'Backing Your Family Doctor', undated (accessed 13 August 2026)

policies.statement: Provide loans to support local GPs to buy into practices

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that youth unemployment continues to rise, with many New Zealanders choosing to move overseas in search of better job opportunities. It believes that expanding the Apprenticeship Boost will provide tradies and young people with greater support as they learn and build their careers in NZ.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would extend employer payments from one year to two years at $500 a month from 1 July 2028. It would also provide a $1000 toolbox grant to help new apprentices cover the cost of tools, kit, uniform and course materials from 1 July 2027. Eligibility for the Apprenticeship Boost would also be extended to include five new trades; road construction, water and sanitary engineering, personal services, sales and marketing, and sports and recreation, with a structured mentoring programme piloted, also from July next year.  This party estimates that this policy would cost $56.5m a year over four years.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that says that power bills have risen by 20 percent in the last two years. Solar power is the cheapest energy source available; however, high installation and equipment costs remain a large barrier for people. It says this policy would help people with these upfront costs, making cheap power accessible for all.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would create a SolarSaver fund, which includes two new Government-backed, long-term, low-interest finance options. The first loan is a Lines company loan, where you borrow through your local lines company to cover the cost of solar and a battery, repaid via your power bill. The second loan is a Ratepayer Assistance Scheme, a low-interest loan attached to your home covering solar, batteries and other home electrification. Repayments would be set below your power bill savings. A kickstart subsidy of up to $3,000 would be available for low- and middle-income households. The party would also amend power regulations so renters can use plug-in solar panels, with a subsidy available to cover the cost of purchase. Funding would come from the Government's Gas Security Fund. This party estimates that this policy would cost $160 million over four years.

citations.title: 'Labour's Solar Saver', undated (accessed 13 August 2026)

policies.statement: Provide loans for people to purchase solar set-ups for their homes

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that small business owners spend too much time chasing overdue invoices. Owners work hard to grow their businesses, and risk their own money along the way. Small businesses deserve to be paid on time.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would introduce legislation enforcing big companies to pay small businesses within 15 days for invoices under $25,000. The party would also restore the disclosure requirements in the Business Payment Practices Act 2023 so companies must publish how quickly they pay. This would be introduced within the first 100 days of taking office, and is part of a $1.56bn small business package over four years.

policies.statement: Introduce legislation to pay small business owners within 15 days of their invoice

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that small businesses make up 97 percent of all New Zealand businesses. If they have more opportunities, the NZ economy will benefit as a whole.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would break up large contracts for government work into smaller jobs, making it more accessible to bid for work. It would also investigate how government agencies can safely share information between each other so small business owners can concentrate on running their business rather than providing details they have already submitted.

citations.title: 'Small Business First', undated (accessed 13 August 2026)

policies.statement: Set a target for 15 percent of government contracts to go to NZ small businesses and start-ups

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that tax credits for equipment will improve cash flow for small businesses so they can continue to grow. It will also mean small businesses can replace essential equipment sooner rather than having to wait for the adequate finances they need.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would lift the low-value asset write-off threshold from $1,000 to $10,000 for businesses with annual revenue below $10 million, from 1 July 2027. This means investments up to $10,000 would be wiped off from the tax bills of small businesses.  This party estimates that this policy would cost $1.56bn over four years.

policies.statement: Offer up to $10,000 in tax credits for small businesses purchasing equipment

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that that reaching the current $60,000 threshold for GST registration adds an extra 15% on prices that small businesses charge their customers. Lifting the threshold means that businesses don't have to worry about losing customers due to higher costs, or spend time filing GST returns.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would lift the GST registration threshold from $60,000 to $80,000 from 1 July 2028.

citations.title: 'Labour's Small Business Action Plan', undated (accessed 13 August 2026)

policies.statement: Increase compulsory GST registration for businesses to $80,000

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that it is possible to return to a positive operating balance without shrinking the economy.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value:
This party would restore the OBEGAL (operating balance before gains and losses) fiscal measurement, and removing OBEGALx, the measure used by the current government which excludes ACC revenue and expenses. 
This party aims to return New Zealand to an OBEGAL surplus in 2029/2030, using the same timing forecast in Budget 2026.

policies.statement: Ensure government balance sheet is in surplus by 2029/2030

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that the country’s debt burden should not be shouldered by future generations, making it vital to invest in infrastructure and productive capacity.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would aim to reduce net debt to around 20 percent of GDP (gross domestic product) over time. It says net debt gives a better picture of the government’s overall fiscal position because it recognises that the government owns financial assets as well as has liabilities. At the same time, it would still prioritise investment to support economic growth.

citations.title: 'Labour will back Kiwis and grow the economy ', 23 August 2026 (accessed 24 August 2026)
'Fiscal Strategy', 23 August 2026 (accessed 24 August 2026)

policies.statement: Reduce New Zealand's debt levels to around 20 percent of GDP

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that New Zealand should be investing now for a more productive future by reducing the future debt burden and investing in key capital projects like ferries, hospitals and schools.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would hold core Crown expenditure and revenue at around 33% of GDP (gross domestic product) when a capital gains tax is fully implemented.

citations.title: 'Labour will back Kiwis and grow the economy ', 23 August 2026 (accessed 24 August 2026)

policies.statement: Create a GDP target for core Crown spending and revenue

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that New Zealanders should be able to see the trade-offs governments are making in their budgets, no matter who is in power. Understanding the costs of a particular commitment can help political parties and citizens.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would establish a new Parliamentary Budget Office to provide independent analysis of the government's finances and every party's spending commitments.

citations.title: 'Labour will back Kiwis and grow the economy ', 23 August 2026 (accessed 24 August 2026)

policies.statement: Establish an independent body to monitor government and party spending

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that monetary policy should be consistent with two objectives: maintaining stable prices over the medium term and maximum sustainable employment. It says keeping inflation in the target band is critical to household budgets, business planning and investment, and prolonged unemployment stops the economy from reaching its full potential.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would restore the Reserve Bank's dual mandate of price stability and maximum sustainable employment.

citations.title: 'Labour will back Kiwis and grow the economy ', 23 August 2026 (accessed 24 August 2026)
'Fiscal Strategy', 23 August 2026 (accessed 24 August 2026)

policies.statement: Restore the Reserve Bank's mandate around prices and employment

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that a government cannot measure its success without considering whether it results in poorer outcomes for New Zealanders’ lives.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would restore wellbeing reporting to the Public Finance Act, to take into account the social as well as fiscal impact of its decisions. These wellbeing measures would be used alongside traditional economic measures.

'Fiscal Strategy', 23 August 2026 (accessed 24 August 2026)

policies.statement: Restore wellbeing reporting to the Public Finance Act

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that it is important to help parents keep their children safe from online harm, but any law would need to be fit for purpose.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would support the bill through its first reading and see it go to select committee before the election.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that it opposes the current government’s plan to lift fuel excise taxes by 22 cents a litre over the next term. It argues that while international oil prices and inflation remains high, higher fuel taxes would affect the entire economy. The government has since confirmed it will not go ahead with the first 12c stage of the fuel tax increase in January.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would not increase fuel excise tax over the next three years to stop price pressure increasing. The fuel excise tax is a key source of transport funding for projects such as the Roads of National Significance programme, some of which have been slowed down in response to the changing economic climate.

policies.statement: Oppose a fuel excise tax in the next term

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that the cost of living is too high to allow for a GST hike and is calling on the government to confirm that it will not raise GST next year. This is in response to the National Party's pledge not to introduce any new taxes before this election.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would ensure GST is not increased in 2027 to ensure the price of basic items does not become unaffordable in the current climate.

citations.title: 'National refuses to rule out GST hike', 27 August 2026 (accessed 27 August 2026)

policies.statement: Rule out raising GST in 2027

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that supporting Māori to get into work, retrain or find a better job is good for everyone. This programme was cut by the current government; it would be reintroduced to help Māori gain practical skills and qualifications for real jobs.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would establish a contestable, Māori-led fund to deliver practical skills training. It's estimated up to 3000 Māori would benefit from the programme, which would include a wide variety of trades and have no age limit. This party estimates that this policy would cost $21m a year.

citations.title: 'Labour is backing Maori into skilled work', 29 August 2026 (accessed 01 September 2026)

policies.statement: Introduce a Maori-led job training programme and fund

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that graduate nurses are being trained here, but because of a lack of job openings, too many are being forced to look overseas instead of starting their careers in New Zealand. The pressure on the health system from the shortage of nurses spills over into patient healthcare.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would guarantee a job for every eligible New Zealand-trained nursing graduate, affecting about 2400 nurses. It would also address pressure on primary care because of the nursing shortage by doubling the funding available through the current recruitment subsidy. The current rate for rural nurses would be lifted from $20,000 to $40,000 and it would rise from $15,000 to $30,000 for nurses in urban areas. This party estimates that this policy would cost $525m.

policies.statement: Guarantee jobs for NZ-trained graduate nurses

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that strongly opposes the Government’s proposal for permanent youth "boot camps," military-style academies run by Oranga Tamariki for serious young offenders. A 12-month pilot finished in July and the party says harmful behaviour has prompted some participants to leave and serve their sentence in mainstream youth justice facilities. The party notes this will not be an option for future young offenders, and also that the majority of participants reoffended within a year.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would reject a bill currently before Parliament allowing the military-style academies for serious young offenders to continue.

citations.title: 'National must scrap its failed boot camps', 1 September 2026 (accessed 01 September 2026)

policies.statement: Stop running youth offender boot camps

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that the current 'Move On' bill criminalises people for sleeping rough when they have no other option. The bill, introduced as a means of maintaining public order, would require disruptive individuals to leave an area for up to 24 hours or risk a fine or prison. The party says while the bill has been somewhat amended, it still does nothing to fix homelessness, which is only fixed with stable housing.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would push to amend the bill at committee stage to remove rough sleeping and begging from the legislation entirely.

citations.title: 'Move on Bill still punishes the homeless', 3 September 2026 (accessed 07 September 2026)

policies.statement: Remove rough sleepers from "Move On" bill

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that the Emissions Trading Scheme is broken, due to the carbon price being too low to drive meaningful emissions reductions. The current ETS also makes it cheaper to plant exotic forests than to grow food.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would review the ETS so it maintains a genuine price on emissions. It will stand by the Paris Agreement and aim to restore certainty to the carbon market. It will focus on changes that incentivise genuine reductions rather than relying on offsets, reconsider the role of forestry and develop new rules to prevent whole-farm conversions. New forestry registrations in the ETS will be paused while the work is done.

citations.title: 'Labour to accelerate climate action', 8 September 2026 (accessed 08 September 2026)

policies.statement: Review the Emissions Trading Scheme

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that AI holds great potential to increase productivity but also carries risks in the form of job losses, harmful content, or a lack of accountability around intellectual property. There is also the risk of data centres driving up energy costs.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would introduce a number of measures including an Office of AI, which would sit within the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, with a senior minister attached. As well as co-ordinating AI policy across government, the office would develop standards for responsible AI use and create a long-term workforce plan. It would also look at government procurement, emerging risks and opportunities and copyright protection from AI. An online safety regulator within the Department for Internal Affairs would be set up.

policies.statement: Create an office to help safely guide the use of AI

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that AI holds great potential to increase productivity but also carries risks in the form of job losses, harmful content, energy use by data centres, and a lack of accountability around intellectual property. People, small businesses, schools and communities must be able to access and share in the benefits of AI.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would launch a $2 million a year fund to help small businesses and community organisations adopt AI safely. It would also boost AI adoption and extend MBIE's AI Advisory pilot to $3 million a year, as part of a wider AI policy. A team would be created to help schools adapt to AI.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that AI holds great potential to increase productivity but also carries risks in the form of job losses, harmful content, or a lack of accountability around intellectual property. The party says data centres must pay their own way without additional costs on households or businesses.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value:
This party would ensure data centres are responsible for their own connection costs and finding their own renewable energy supply. Centres would also have to use water efficiently and reduce electricity demand during peak periods, to ensure they don't drive up costs for households and businesses. 
These measures are part of a wider policy aimed at harnessing the benefits of AI while still ensuring safely and accountability.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that protecting NZ's data sovereignty in the age of AI is a huge challenge, but New Zealanders should have a say over how their data, and data collected here, is stored, governed and used. Creative people must be able to retain control over work used by AI, and be paid for it.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would strengthen control over NZ data, and would work with iwi and hapū on how Māori data is collected, owned, governed and used.  A copyright framework would be developed with creators, publishers and tech companies so creators control and are paid for work used by AI.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that immigration should be planned around what New Zealand needs, in a way that's fair to everyone here and everyone who comes. It should attract the skills and talent our country needs, while protecting migrants from exploitation and supporting their arrival.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would set up a citizenship pathway for children born in NZ. It would also protect humanitarian appeals against deportation and review parent visa, health, and English-language rules. This is part of a wider immigration policy which aims to treat migrants with decency and make NZ an attractive place for talent, while reflecting the country's workforce, housing and infrastructure needs.

citations.title: 'Labour to ensure an immigration system that works for New Zealand', 11 September 2026 (accessed 12 September 2026)

policies.statement: Establish a citizenship pathway for migrants' children born in NZ

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that immigration is a balance between the country's needs and the need to attract talent and skills. To do this, NZ should protect migrants from exploitation and support their arrival, while ensuring that our immigration settings consider NZ's workforce, housing and infrastructure needs.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would protect migrants from exploitation by enabling them to move between accredited employers after three months, rather than tying their visa to one employer.  By strengthening the Accredited Employer Work Visa scheme, and improving support in their communities, migrants would be less vulnerable,

citations.title: 'Labour to ensure an immigration system that works for New Zealand', 11 September 2026 (accessed 12 September 2026)

policies.statement: Allow migrants to move between accredited employers

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that NZ's immigration policies are a balance between the country's needs and making NZ a place that is attractive to skilled migrants and where they can have confidence in the system. Migrants should be encouraged to put down roots by increasing the length of time they must stay before applying for permanent residence.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would encourage a longer stay by extending the eligibility period for permanent residence from two years to four. This would be supported by a programme of NZ orientation and civic education, to strengthen social cohesion.

citations.title: 'Labour to ensure an immigration system that works for New Zealand', 11 September 2026 (accessed 12 September 2026)

policies.statement: Extend permanent residence eligibility to four years

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that immigration should be planned around what New Zealand needs, in a way that's fair to everyone here and everyone who comes. Migrants bring much-needed energy and skills but they need clear and predictable rules to attract them, and protection from exploitation, while ensuring NZ has the capacity for them.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would introduce a set of measures including the setting of immigration goals through a Government Policy Statement that reflects the country's workforce, housing and infrastructure needs. The wider policy includes extending the length of time needed for permanent residence, allowing migrants to move more easily between accredited employers, and offering better community support.

citations.title: 'Labour to ensure an immigration system that works for New Zealand', 11 September 2026 (accessed 12 September 2026)

policies.statement: Create an immigration statement that reflects NZ's needs

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that Kiwisaver is crucial to building a secure future and a key source of investment for the economy. However, more than a million working-age KiwiSaver members are not contributing at all, while 83,400 are on a savings suspension. This party would take the government's proposed Kiwisaver plan and make it more flexible for workers, particularly those under financial pressure.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would make KiwiSaver more flexible and therefore more attractive for Kiwis to save. It would make employer contributions compulsory and lift them to 6 percent by 2032. It would extend employer contributions to workers over 65, and encompass the self-employed and those on parental leave.  The default employee contribution would be set at 4 percent and the minimum contribution would be removed. Employer contributions would continue even when employees reduced or paused their own contributions. Contracts that absorb employer Kiwisaver contributions into total salaries would be banned.

citations.title: 'Labour will strengthen Kiwisaver for future generations', 13 September 2026 (accessed 14 September 2026)

policies.statement: Make Kiwisaver more flexible for workers

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that New Zealanders are paying too much for basic items such as food. It believes a crackdown is needed on big companies who charge excessive prices for essential goods or services. It notes that there is no legal test for excessive or unfair pricing in NZ.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would adjust legislation to address price gouging and give the Commerce Commission to new powers investigate what dominant companies are charging and take them to court. The legislation would only include industries that supply essentials such as food and groceries, banking and insurance, telecommunications, energy, fuel and investment. The law will apply where a company has enough market power that customers can't realistically switch, suppliers have nowhere else to go, or new competitors struggle to enter a market. Companies found to have overcharged consumers will face penalties and be ordered to make repayments. The policy would only touch big players with significant market powers, not small businesses.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that negligent employers need to be held accountable for workplace deaths. New Zealand has one of the highest workplace death rates in the developed world and yet employers cannot be held accountable for corporate homicide. Making this an offence would serve as a stronger incentive to take workplace safety seriously.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would hold introducing an offence for corporate homicide to encourage industries and employers to put in place adequate safety systems.

policies.statement: Introduce corporate homicide as an offence

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that retirees would wait up to nine months to get their own money back after they leave their village under a new National policy, and it excludes those already living in villages. Retired people and their families should receive a payout promptly.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would introduce a law requiring village operators to pay residents or their estates 10 percent of what they are owed within five working days, with the balance paid within three months. This would cover existing as well as future residents. A targeted exemption may be available if a village operator is in financial difficulty.

policies.statement: Ensure retirement villages pay residents out more quickly when they leave

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that New Zealanders are not paying a fair price for groceries. The country needs a more competitive supermarket sector, which is currently dominated by two players who favour their own retail stores at the disadvantage of smaller players.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would would make Woolworths and Foodstuffs run their­­ wholesale supply businesses independently from their retail stores. It would also give Kiwi grocers the right to buy their stock from any wholesaler they choose, and free up small players to void anti-competitive arrangements that keep their prices high. Rebate and data deals would be made more transparent.

attributes.value: This party says that NZ needs to have an independent foreign policy, focused on Pacific partners. The country needs friendship and allies with close partners, particularly in Australia and the Pacific, in uncertain times.

attributes.name: How

Climate change and economic development are major challenges in this region, and NZ needs to support neighbouring countries with these challenges.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would work towards a Pacific agreement on climate mitigation, adaptation and displacement. It would specifically focus on Tuvalu and Kiribati on long-term plans for climate adaptation and possible resettlement.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that NZ has a reputation as an honest and independent country which defends international law. When human rights abuses and war create genocide and ethnic cleansing, NZ must have the moral clarity to speak up, specifically regarding the situation in Palestine.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would recognise the state of Palestine at the UN and place economic sanctions on Israel. It would ensure that the ACC and NZ Super Funds are divested from holdings in the Palestinian occupied territories, according to the list prepared by the UN. It would support South Africa at its case at the International Court of Justice, saying that Israel is breaching the Genocide Convention.

attributes.value: This party says that the world is more uncertain and more competitive than at any time in recent memory, and old alliances and assumptions are under real strain.  It is possible to trade as well as disagree with a country. Public support for globalisations is decreasing, but the answer is agreements with other markets, not tariffs.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would continue to pursue trade agreements, especially with new markets in Africa and South America. It would prioritise relationships with ASEAN countries, the EU and Canada. It would make it easier to move money and data across the Pacific.

attributes.name: Why

As a small country, NZ needs to do its part to work on goals like the Paris agreement and the care of Antarctica.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would support and retain membership of the UN, World Trade Organisation, International Court of Justice and International Criminal Court. It would continue to fulfil the responsibilities and requirements of the Paris Agreement and Antarctic Treaty and advocate for international scientific cooperation. It would support the country of Ukraine in its war against Russia.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that student debt can hang over people for years, making it harder to save for a home, start a family or plan for the future. In launching this policy, this party hopes to encourage students to stay and work in NZ, rather than going overseas.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value:
This party would write off 10% of eligible student loan balances. Students already finished and repaying their loan from 1 April 2027, and to current or future students three years after their studies, as long as they spent those years in NZ, would be eligible for the write-off. Eligible people would have to be up-to-date with their payments and have not received the now-defunct Fees Free incentive. Smaller loans of $2000 or less would be fully written off after the three years.  
 This party estimates that this policy would cost nearly $40m a year once fully running in 2031.

Similar moves in Australia mean car repairs by independent mechanics are 25% cheaper than dealerships.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value:
This party would enable independent mechanics and petrol stations to access manuals, software and tools to fix modern cars. This effectively gives drivers the right of repair.
This is part of a wider policy on market competition, which includes giving the Commerce Commission the power to investigate fuel prices, and freezing fuel excise taxes for three years.

attributes.value: This party would require airlines to show the real price of airfares up front for price comparison. It would also increase transparency by requiring airlines to publicly report on profits and performance data, such as delays. Automatic refunds would kick in when flights are cancelled or significantly changed, and customers would have to be compensated or reimbursed when checked baggage is significantly delayed.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that smart phones are one of the parenting challenges of our time. Tech companies have too much power over what we see and fake images are harder to spot. Many parents worry about what their children are seeing or if they are being bullied. More responsibility should be placed on the companies making money from these platforms.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would introduce more digital regulation to Parliament within the first 100 days, including no social media accounts for under-16s. Social media companies would be legally responsible for policing this, and a new digital duty of care will be introduced with stronger privacy and other protections for those under 18. Other action would include more control for users over their feeds, and stronger rules around deepfakes and non-consensual sexual images. An independent digital regulator will be created, with powers to take action against companies that break the rules.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that that parents and schools need help to keep kids safer online, keep them active and prevent screen addiction. Technology has its place but children need help to regulate their consumption and to protect themselves against online harm.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would provide more support for schools with digital technology. This includes clear expectations on screentime and a continuation of the ban on mobile phones at school. Schools and parents would be helped to find and use online-safety tools, including an education AI app. This is part of a wider policy on AI use, tighter social media regulation and a ban on social media accounts for under-16-year-olds.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that patients are waiting too long, emergency departments are overcrowded, and nurses and doctors are under enormous pressure. Delays in ED are often due to a lack of beds in hospital wards and staffing issues.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would order an immediate review of hospital wait times and bed shortages, and also the safety issues linked to emergency departments. This party believes that the pressure on EDs can be reduced and more hospital beds can be opened up with action at hospital and community level. Its wider health plan includes adding more nurses, funding three free GP visits annually, and training more extended-care paramedics to treat people at home.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that schools are seeing more children with complex learning needs. Teachers are doing an incredible job, but they can't do it alone. This party says that schools are struggling to find the funds for learning support.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would fund 1,000 extra teacher aides to give more individual support for students who need it, and more help in busy classrooms. The party would also use the 2022 Highest Needs Review to help identify gaps in learning support. This policy would cost $80m over four years, which this party says would give schools more certainty and teacher aides more job security.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that state house and community housing tenants who struggle to save for a first home deposit, even when they are working, on top of their rent.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would introduce rent-to-buy housing for eligible Kāinga Ora state house and community housing tenants who are working. Tenants would have $100 of their weekly rent placed in a trust account to accumulate towards a 5% deposit. They will also be able to access an expanded First Home Loan scheme, which enables people to obtain a mortgage with a five percent deposit. The combined income cap would be lifted to $300,000 and more banks would be brought into the scheme. This party would ensure that proceeds from public homes sold through the rent-to-buy scheme would be reinvested into more public housing.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that with the cost of living being so high, people are struggling to save the deposit to buy their first home.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would expand First Home Loans scheme to more people and keep the amount required for a deposit at five percent of the loan. The income cap for eligibility would be lifted to $300,000 per household, and more banks would be brought into the scheme. This party would also introduce rent-to-buy scheme to lower the barriers to home ownership for working state house and community housing tenants. It would put the proceeds from public homes sold through the rent-to-buy scheme into more public housing.
